questions.question: You are provided 1 M Tris buffer. How will you dilute this to make 500 ml 0.1 M buffer
questions.solution_html:
• You are provided with 1 M Tris Buffer. How will you dilute this to make 500 ml 0.1 M buffer ? /
  • N1V1 = N2V2 N1 = 1M; V1 = X N2 = 0.1 M, V2 = 500 ml
  • X = 50 ml. Take 50 ml stock solution in a 500 ml standard flask and make up this to 500 ml using distilled
  • water.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the equivalence point and the end point in a titration?
questions.solution_html:
• What is the key difference between the equivalence point and the endpoint in a titration? /
  • Equivalence point: The point in a titration where the amount of added titrant is chemically equivalent to the
  • amount of analyte in the sample, based on the reaction’s stoichiometry. It is a theoretical, chemical concept.
  • End point: The point in a titration where a visible change, most commonly a color change in the indicator, is
  • observed. It is an experimental, practical observation.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: observed. It is an experimental, practical observation.

  • (CCDs) and Charge-Injection Devices (CIDs)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: (CCDs) and Charge-Injection Devices (CIDs)

questions.question: Recall the concepts of Molarity and ppm.
questions.solution_html:
• Recall the concepts of molarity and ppm /
  • Molarity- Number of moles of solute per litre of total solution. Molarity = Moles of solute/V olume of solution
  • in litres. Moles of solute = mass of solute (g)/molar mass of solute.
  • PPM – Parts per Million. Amount of solute per one million parts of the total solution. Divide mass or volume
  • of the solute by the total mass or volume of the solution and then multiply the result with one million (solute
  • in mg, volume of solution in microliter)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: in mg, volume of solution in microliter)

questions.question: Explain briefly electromagnetic spectrum.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain briefly electromagnetic spectrum. /
  • The full range of all electromagnetic radiation, ordered by frequency or wavelength. The spectrum is divided

  • frequency, these are: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. The

questions.question: What is a buffer. What are the factors that affect buffering capacity?
questions.solution_html:
• What is a buffer. What are the factors that affect buffering capacity?
  • A solution that can resist pH change on addition of small amounts of acid/alkali. Mixture of weak acid and its
  • conjugate base or a weak base and its conjugate acid.
  • Factors affecting buffering capacity - Concentration of buffer component (Higher concentration - greater
  • buffering capacity), ratio of acid to base (highest when concentration of acid and base components are equal),
  • pH (highest when pH is equal to pKa), temperature and ionic strength
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: pH (highest when pH is equal to pKa), temperature and ionic strength

questions.question: Give a brief note on methyl orange and bromothymol blue as visual indicators in acid-alkali titrations.
questions.solution_html:
• Give a brief note on methyl orange and bromothymol blue as visual indicators in acid-alkali titrations.
  • /
  • Methyl orange and bromothymol blue are pH indicators that change color in acid -base titrations, but they are
  • suitable for different pH ranges and types of reactions. Methyl Orange: Red in acidic solutions and yellow in
  • basic solutions. pH range - 3.1-4.4. Best for titrations with an equivalence point in the acidic range, such as a
  • strong acid being titrated with a weak base. Bromothymol Blue: Yellow in acidic solutions and blue in alkaline
  • solutions. pH range- 6.0-7.6. Best for titrations where the equivalence point is near neutral pH, such as a strong
  • acid with a strong base.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: acid with a strong base.

questions.question: What is the principle of a UV-Visible spectrophotometer?
questions.solution_html:
• What is the principle of UV-Visible spectrophotometer? /
  • Beer-Lambert Law – The absorbance of a solution is directly proportional to its concentration and the path
  • length of the light through the solution. The instrument works by passing a beam of UV or visible light through
  • a sample, and a detector measures the amount of light absorbed at each wavelength. This absorption causes
  • electrons in the molecules to transition from a lower to a higher energy state.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: electrons in the molecules to transition from a lower to a higher energy state.

questions.question: What is an electronic balance? What are the precautions to be taken while using an electronic balance?
questions.solution_html:
• What is an electronic balance? What are the precautions to be taken while using an electronic balance?
  • /
  • An electronic balance is a high -precision digital scale used in laboratories to measure the mass of a substance
  • with a high degree of accuracy. Unlike older mechanical balances, electronic balances use a force-measurement
  • transducer to convert the force exerted by the mass into an electrical signal, which is then displayed as a digital
  • reading
  • Precautions- Ensure the balance is placed on a level, stable surface, away from vibrations, direct sunlight.
  • Inspect the balance to ensure it is clean and free of any debris. Use the leveling screws to make sure the balance
  • is level. Switch on the device and wait for 5 minutes to warm up the instrument. Select the correct unit of
  • weighing. Never place the salt directly onto the balance pan, place the clean, dry weighing vessel. Tare to zero
  • before weighing
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: before weighing

questions.question: Explain the measurement of p H using litmus paper and p H paper.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the measurement of pH using litmus paper and pH paper. /
  • Litmus paper- just whether solution is acidic or alkaline. Dip a piece of litmus paper in solution. Observe for
  • colour change. Blue litmus turns red in acid and red litmus turns blue in alkali.
  • pH paper- measurement of ph. Dip a piece of litmus paper in solution or else take a clean glass plate, add a
  • drop of solution. Cut a piece of litmus paper and place near the drop and using a clean rod push paper in to the
  • rod. Observe for colour change.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: rod. Observe for colour change.

questions.question: Explain the various steps in gravimetric analysis.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the various steps in gravimetric analysis. /
  • • Sample preparation: Weigh out a precise amount of the sample and dissolve it in a suitable solvent.
  • • Precipitation: Add a precipitating agent to the sample solution; this agent reacts with the analyte to
  • form an insoluble precipitate
  • • Digestion: Allow the precipitate to digest, this allows for larger, purer crystals to form, which are easier
  • to filter
  • • Filtration: Separate the solid precipitate from the liquid using a filter.
  • • Washing: Wash the precipitate on the filter paper to remove impurities
  • • Drying or Ignition: Dry the precipitate in an oven; this removes any remaining solvent and ensures the
  • final product is pure
  • • Weighing and Calculation
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: • Weighing and Calculation

questions.question: Explain the principle of scattering spectroscopy with special reference to working and use of Raman spectrophotometer.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the principle of scattering spectroscopy with special reference to working and use of Raman
  • spectrophotometer. /
  • When light interacts with a sample, some of it is scattered. While most light undergoes elastic Rayleigh
  • scattering, a small fraction undergoes inelastic Raman scattering, where the scattered photons have a different
  • energy (and therefore frequency) than the incident photons. This difference, known as Raman shift, corresponds
  • to the vibrational modes of the molecule, providing a unique “fingerprint” for chemical identification in a Raman
  • spectrophotometer.
  • • Working- Light source, sample interaction, spectrometer, filtering, dispersion, detection, and spectrum
  • analysis
  • • Uses- Quality control, medical diagnostics, forensics, material identification, and in the pharmaceutical
  • industry.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: industry.
